newsitem.title: USA: Silver supply deficit seen smaller in 97 - CPM.
newsitem.headline: Silver supply deficit seen smaller in 97 - CPM.

text.p: The supply of newly refined silver onto world markets is forecast to rise by 9.4 percent to 570.6 million ounces in 1997, while fabrication demand could rise a further 2.8 percent to 739.4 million ounces, New York based industry consultants CPM Group said Tuesday.

But there will still be a deficit between supply and demand of around 168.8 million ounces, even though the deficit will be smaller than the 197.8 million ounces seen in 1996 and the 176.0 million ounces in 1995.

"Expectations are that continuing deficits in newly refined silver supplies relative to fabrication demand will eventually lead to a period of significantly higher prices," CPM Group managing director, Jeffrey Christian told analysts at the publication of the Group's 1997 silver survey.

Silver mine production expanded 3.5 percent in 1996 as output in Mexico and Peru rose significantly. In 1997 mine output is projected to rise 11.1 percent to 400 million ounces, spurred by higher production in Mexico, Peru, the US and some other countries, the report said.

Secondary supply from old scrap, coin melt, and South Asian dishoarding rose 2.3 pct last year to 148.9 million ounces but in 1997 silver flowing from these sources could reach 157.2 million ounces, up 5.6 pct.
Silver use in all industrial applications totaled 719.5 million ounces in 1996, an increase of 3.8 pct from 1995, and in 1997 could rise a further 2.8 pct to 739.4 million ounces.

The strongest growth last year was seen in jewelry and silverware demand which jumped 5.7 pct to 255 million ounces but growth may moderate this year to 3.0 pct with jewelry and and silverware manufacturers absorbing 262.7 million ounces.
Silver use in photographic films, papers and prints rose 4.1 pct in 1996 to 230.2 million ounces and this year may rise 3.2 pct to 237.6 million ounces, CPM Group said.
"The emerging markets once again fuelled the expansion in fabrication demand for silver," Christian said. Indian demand surged 13.9 pct in 1996 to 109.9 million, after two years of decline.
But transitional economies are also expected to become large net importers of silver in the next few years, the report said.
"The silver market in China is growing increasingly tighter," CPM Group research director, Joseph Rosta said.
"Silver use may have expanded 15.5 pct to approximately 104 million ounces in 1996, while mine output was estimated at 6.97 million ounces, up four percent.
"China already appears to be importing the bulk of Poland's silver output, and it continues to draw down silver inventories seized by the government after 1949."
Silver consumption in the US rose 7.7 pct in 1996 to 146.7 million ounces, the report notes.
Since 1992, year-over-year total US fabrication demand has been expanding at a compounded average rate of 5.4 pct.
